uncited: Self-calibration via the absolute dual quadric is a method to recover metric (Euclidean) camera intrinsics and 3D structure from a projective reconstruction obtained from uncalibrated images.
It solves the ambiguity of projective reconstruction by imposing constraints on the absolute dual quadric $\Omega^*$, which is invariant under Euclidean transformations.
Unlike methods requiring known calibration targets, this approach derives intrinsic parameters solely from the geometry of the scene across multiple views.

It sets itself apart from direct linear methods by leveraging the global constraint of the absolute dual quadric to upgrade a projective structure to a metric one, building on [Camera Matrix Decomposition](3164-camera-matrix-decomposition.md).
- A set of $n$ projective camera matrices $\hat{P}_i$ for $i=1 \dots n$, derived from a projective factorization of the point correspondence matrix.
Each $\hat{P}_i$ is a $3 \times 4$ matrix.
- Assumptions on intrinsic parameters (see Parameters).
- Metric camera matrices $P_i^M = K_i [R_i | t_i]$.
- The rectifying transformation $H$ (Projective Distortion Matrix).
Partitioned into $\hat{P}_i = [S_i | s_i]$, where $S_i$ is $3 \times 3$ and $s_i$ is $3 \times 1$.
The relationship between the metric and projective camera matrices is $P_i^M = \hat{P}_i H$.
- Principal point at image center: $\varpi_{13}^* = \varpi_{23}^* = 0$.
- Aspect ratio equal to 1: $\varpi_{11}^* = \varpi_{22}^*$.
These assumptions leave only the focal length as a variable.
Collect the linear constraints from all $m$ views into an overdetermined linear system $A \mathbf{x} = 0$, where $\mathbf{x}$ contains the independent elements of $\Omega^*$.
The system has dimensions $4m \times 10$ (since $\Omega^*$ is symmetric $4 \times 4$ with 10 unique elements).
Solve for $\mathbf{x}$ using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD).
Reconstruct the $4 \times 4$ matrix $\Omega^*$ from $\mathbf{x}$.
Since $\Omega^* = H \tilde{I} H^T$, and $\tilde{I} = \text{diag}(1,1,1,0)$, $H$ can be found via Cholesky-like decomposition or by solving for the parameters directly.
where $K_1$ is the calibration matrix of the first camera and $p$ is the vector from step 2/4.
Specifically, from $\Omega^* = \begin{bmatrix} \varpi_1^* & -\varpi_1^* p \\ -p^T \varpi_1^* & p^T \varpi_1^* p \end{bmatrix}$, extract $\varpi_1^*$ and $p$.
Decompose $P_i^M$ into $K_i [R_i | t_i]$ using standard decomposition (e.g., [Camera Matrix Decomposition](3164-camera-matrix-decomposition.md)).
- The method assumes constant intrinsic parameters across all views.
- The assumptions (zero skew, square pixels, centered principal point) are critical for the linear formulation.
- **Time Complexity:** Solving the linear system via SVD is $O(m)$ for the construction of $A$ and $O(1)$ for the SVD of a fixed-size matrix ($4m \times 10$).
The decomposition of $H$ and upgrade is $O(m)$.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(m)$ to store the camera matrices and the constraint matrix $A$.
Sensitive to noise in projective reconstruction.
- **When to use:** When a projective reconstruction is available and the camera has fixed, simple intrinsics (e.g., standard digital cameras with known principal point).
- **When not to use:** When intrinsics are unknown and vary, or when high precision is required without subsequent non-linear refinement.
The method was developed in the context of structure from motion and camera calibration, specifically as part of the stratified reconstruction approach.
It relies on the geometric invariance of the absolute dual quadric under Euclidean transformations.
